title: Communication Network Analysis
short_description: Learn how a communication company traces how devices are connected, checks whether parts of the network stay connected, and finds the fastest and most cost-effective ways for information to travel between nodes using graph algorithms.

real_world_context.problem: A communication company operates a wide network of towers, routers and switching centers. Engineers must determine which devices a signal can reach from a given source, check whether the network has broken into separate regions after a failure, find the lowest-latency route for data between two nodes, decide which links to lease so that every node is connected at the minimum cost, and precompute fast routes between every pair of nodes.
real_world_context.why_it_matters: Graph algorithms let communication companies keep large networks reachable and reliable, reduce link and leasing cost, and answer route and latency questions quickly as the number of devices and subscribers grows.

learning_objectives: Represent a communication network as an undirected graph using an adjacency list.
Traverse a network with Breadth-First Search (BFS) to map which devices a signal can reach from a source node.
Traverse a network with Depth-First Search (DFS) to detect whether parts of the network have become separate regions.
Use Dijkstra's algorithm to find the lowest-latency route between two nodes.
Use Kruskal's algorithm to build a minimum-cost backbone network that connects every node.
Use Floyd-Warshall to precompute the shortest route between every pair of nodes.
prerequisites: Introduction to graphs and adjacency lists
completion_message: You have completed the Communication Network Analysis mission. You have learned how graph traversals, shortest-path algorithms and minimum-spanning-tree algorithms can be used to keep a communication network reachable, reliable and cost-effective.
